vignette:
Mateo is 26, but he moves with the caution of a much older man. Two years have passed since the events that led him to the United States, but time has done little to soften the rigid set of his shoulders or the constant, scanning motion of his eyes. The divorce papers, finalized six months ago, sit in a drawer, a testament to the life that was dismantled in the aftermath. He works as a maid for a commercial cleaning company, the late-night solitude of empty office buildings offering a fragile truce with a world he has come to see as a landscape of hidden threats.

It had started with a car, a dark green sedan with a dent in the passenger-side door. The men who pulled him from the street in his home country wore uniforms, their authority absolute and unquestionable. The days that followed are not a coherent narrative in his mind, but a series of disjointed sensory fragments: the rough texture of a concrete floor against his cheek, the blinding glare of a single bare bulb, the sudden, sharp impacts on his body that came without warning. He never knew when the next touch would be a blow, and that uncertainty has burrowed deep into his nervous system. Now, any dark sedan he sees on his commute is that car, and his heart begins to pound with a force that makes him feel he might collapse on the sidewalk. He has to turn his head, fix his gaze on a distant building, and breathe through the metallic taste of fear until the car is gone.

This fear dictates the shape of his life. At work, the sight of the building’s security guard making his nightly rounds sends a jolt of ice through his veins. Mateo has learned the man’s schedule not for efficiency, but for avoidance. He will duck into the nearest supply closet, the smell of bleach and industrial soap a strange comfort, and wait until the sound of footsteps recedes. He knows, rationally, that this guard is not one of them, but the uniform erases all distinction. The same retreat happens at home. He can no longer watch the evening news; any footage of police officers or soldiers, even in a distant country, brings the memory rushing back with the force of a physical blow. A brief glimpse of a uniform on screen is enough to make him feel the rough texture of the concrete floor against his cheek again. His colleagues have learned not to approach him from behind; a friendly hand on his shoulder once caused him to cry out and spin around, fists raised, leaving a chasm of embarrassed silence between them. He feels threatened by anyone who gets too close, a stranger on the bus or a person asking for directions becoming a potential aggressor in his mind.

The nights offer no respite. Sleep is shallow, punctuated by two or three awakenings where he finds himself sitting bolt upright in bed, straining to hear a threat in the quiet hum of the refrigerator. He must get up, check the lock on his door, and peer through the blinds before his racing heart will allow him to lie back down. His only reliable comfort is the sharp, acrid pull of a cigarette, a ritual he turns to whenever a memory ambushes him or the walls of his small apartment feel like they are closing in. His ex-wife, Ana, had tried to get him to talk about what happened. But being reminded by others, or seeing a uniform on the news, felt like being pushed back into that dark room, and he would shut down, his silence a wall she could no longer scale. "You're here," she had said before she left, "but you're not."

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment of unexpected joy. Last week, at his sister's house, watching his young nephew chase bubbles in the backyard, a genuine laugh escaped him. The feeling was so foreign it was immediately followed by a wave of cold panic. Happiness, he had come to believe, was a lapse in security. To feel good was to let his guard down, and to let his guard down was to invite disaster. The terror that followed this simple, pure moment was more profound than any other. He realized he was not just avoiding threats from the outside world, but from his own inner life. He has come to therapy not with any grand hope of being his old self, but with a desperate, quiet plea: to one day be able to laugh without feeling like he is about to die.
